description: Composite three-panel figure: (a) and (b) are twin property plots, (c) is a principle schematic. (a) plots "Stress, Hardening rate (MPa)" (linear, 0-1800, ticks every 200) versus "Effective plastic strain" (0-0.8); legend entries are exactly "Ferrite stress" (filled squares), "Ferrite hardening rate" (open squares), "Bainite stress" (filled triangles), "Bainite hardening rate" (open triangles). Stresses rise monotonically with strain (ferrite from roughly 450 MPa to about 730 MPa; bainite from about 740 MPa to about 1080 MPa) while hardening rates fall steeply (first points between the 1400 and 1800 MPa gridlines, approaching ~150 MPa). Two circled intersections are labelled 0.127 (bainite hardening rate/stress, just above the 800 MPa gridline) and 0.163 (ferrite, between the 400 and 600 MPa gridlines). (b) repeats the format for "Austenite stress"/"Austenite hardening rate" and "Martensite stress"/"Martensite hardening rate" on a 0-5000 MPa axis (ticks every 1000, first martensite point above the 5000 tick); circled intersections are labelled 0.348 (austenite, near the 1000 MPa gridline) and 0.50 (martensite, between the 1000 and 2000 gridlines, closer to 2000). (c) has unnumbered "True strain" (x) and "True stress" (y) axes with dotted "Work hardening rate" and solid "Stress-strain curve" curves intersecting at grey "Necking point" circles; a grey arrow labelled "Higher uniform elongation/tensile strenght" shows that a higher hardening rate shifts necking to larger strain. Together the panels apply the Considere criterion to rank phase hardening: martensite > bainite > austenite > ferrite.

subfigures.description: Line plot of Stress and Hardening rate (MPa, 0-1800) vs Effective plastic strain (0-0.8) with four series: Ferrite stress (filled squares), Ferrite hardening rate (open squares), Bainite stress (filled triangles), Bainite hardening rate (open triangles). Hardening-rate curves decay steeply while stress curves rise gently; circled intersections labelled 0.127 (bainite) and 0.163 (ferrite).

Same plot type for retained austenite and martensite, Stress/Hardening rate (MPa) 0-5000 vs Effective plastic strain 0-0.8; series are Austenite stress (filled squares), Austenite hardening rate (open squares), Martensite stress (filled triangles), Martensite hardening rate (open triangles). Circled intersections labelled 0.348 (austenite) and 0.50 (martensite).

Unnumbered schematic with axes True stress (vertical) and True strain (horizontal). A red solid stress-strain curve and a dashed work-hardening-rate curve intersect at a grey circle labelled Necking point; a second, lower black pair of curves intersects at an earlier necking point. A broad grey arrow labelled 'Higher uniform elongation/tensile strenght' points to the right, indicating larger uniform elongation when the hardening rate is higher.

observations.observation: In (a) the legend prints exactly 'Ferrite stress', 'Ferrite hardening rate', 'Bainite stress' and 'Bainite hardening rate', with hardening-rate series drawn as open symbols and stress series as filled symbols.
In (a) the circled intersection of the bainite hardening-rate and bainite stress curves is labelled with the number 0.127, and that of ferrite with 0.163.

In (b) the circled intersections are labelled 0.348 (austenite curves) and 0.50 (martensite curves); the martensite intersection lies at a much higher stress than the austenite one and at a larger effective plastic strain.

The y-axis scale differs between (a) (0-1800 MPa, ticks every 200) and (b) (0-5000 MPa, ticks every 1000), showing hardening rates of austenite/martensite roughly three times larger than those of ferrite/bainite.
In both (a) and (b) the work-hardening-rate curves decrease monotonically with effective plastic strain while the corresponding stress curves increase monotonically, so the two cross exactly once.
Panel (b) y-axis label is printed as 'Stress, Hardening rate (MPa)' identical to panel (a); neither panel prints error bars or test temperature.

Panel (c) contains the annotations 'Work hardening rate', 'Stress-strain curve', 'Necking point', and the grey arrow text 'Higher uniform elongation/tensile strenght' (spelling as printed); its axes carry tick marks but no numerical values.

The caption states that (a,b) give the work hardening rate and tensile flow stress of ferrite, bainite, retained austenite and martensite phase with plastic strain, and that (c) is the illustration of the Considere criterion to evaluate metallic material mechanical properties (adapted with permission, Copyright 2008, Elsevier).
The citing text states that the hardening rate of martensite is stronger than that of the other phases.
The citing text states necking strains of martensite 0.5, bainite 0.127, ferrite 0.163 and retained austenite 0.348, matching the numbers printed in panels (a) and (b).

According to the Considere criterion described in the citing text, the necking point of a metallic material appears at the intersection of the work hardening rate and the true stress, so a higher work hardening rate gives higher uniform elongation and tensile strength.
The citing text attributes the phase-resolved strengthening contributions extracted in this figure to an ABAQUS/UMAT framework by Dan et al.

unreadable_items: panel (c): axes have tick marks but no numerical scale values printed
panels (a) and (b): no printed values for the maximum hardening rates or for the peak stresses of each phase
panels (a) and (b): no test temperature, strain rate or source-material condition given on the axes or in the legends
